Issued at 208 AM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

Though Tonight:

A recent hand surface analysis revealed a 1003mb surface low 
pressure system centered over southern Wisconsin. A sharp cold 
front extends southwestward through central Iowa and into the 
central Plains toward a secondary surface low centered near the 
Colorado and Kansas border. In the warm sector of the Great 
Lakes cyclone, it is an unseasonably warm night with current 
temperatures at press time in the mid 70s (some 10 degrees 
warmer than typical high temperatures this time of year). A 
strong low-level jet (50-55kt at about 3000 feet AGL per the 
KLOT VWP) is maintaining a few southwesterly surface gusts of 15
to 20 mph early this morning, as well (the Chicago Crib is 
gusting to nearly 40 mph). Taking a step back, the large-scale 
pattern is being driven by a strong Pacific trough digging 
toward the four Corners Region, leading to quasi-zonal flow 
across the central and eastern United States. Over the next 72 
hours, the local weather will be influenced by the trough as it 
evolves eastward with time. 

Based on the current location and speed of the cold front, it 
should move across our local area just after daybreak. Low-level
cold air advection doesn't look particularly noteworthy in our 
area behind the front, a consequence of a low-level pressure col
developing between the departing low pressure system toward the
northeastern US and the surface pressure falls in the Plains. 
In fact, the front may very well stall somewhere near US-24 by 
early afternoon, transitioning into more of a stationary front 
ahead of the trough moving through the southwestern United 
States. Nevertheless, today is still shaping up to be another 
unseasonably warm day with highs in the upper 70s near the 
Wisconsin state line, around 80 near the I-88 and I-80 
corridors, and mid to locally upper 80s in closer proximity to 
the frontal boundary near US-24. Will have to watch for a 
sprinkle or two from mid-morning to early afternoon near the 
front as a plume of modestly steep mid-level lapse rates (around
7 K/km per the 00Z OAX RAOB) coincident with a pocket of mid- 
level moisture (area of ACCAS currently over eastern Nebraska 
and western Iowa) slides through northern Illinois. Given a 
residual pocket of dry low-level air across the area (notably 
below 700 mb, see the 00Z DVN RAOB), will keep the chance of 
measurable precipitation in the 5 to 10% range, again largely 
south of I-80. 

This evening and tonight, the dominant Pacific upper-level 
trough will propagate toward the Four Corners region 
establishing southwesterly low- to mid-level flow from the 
southern Plains toward the Lower Great Lakes. The tightening 
low-level baroclinic zone across the middle Mississippi River 
Valley (partially forced by a building surface high in the 
northern Plains) beneath a parade of upper-level shortwaves will
support the development of several clusters of showers and 
thunderstorms. The current expectation is for the most robust 
activity to remain tied to the highest-quality low-level 
moisture near and south of the front generally from central 
Kansas to central Illinois, through still do expect a healthy 
coverage of showers and storms as far north as the I-88 corridor
from the evening through the overnight hours. Relatively high 
freezing levels (near 14,500 ft AGL) and modest/skinny CAPE 
profiles to limit updraft intensity (weak lapse-rates) should 
otherwise offset a favorable kinematic/shear profile for hail. 
And while the upper-level flow does look extremely unbalanced, 
any synoptic-scale gravity wave formation should tend to be 
offset well north of the instability axis likely mitigating a 
GWAC/damaging wind threat. As a result, current expectations are
for the thunderstorms tonight to be fairly generic with the 
common threats of downpours, occasional lightning strikes, and 
pea to dime size hail. Coverage of activity should wane markedly
by daybreak Wednesday. 


Wednesday into Wednesday night:

On Wednesday, the northern Plains high pressure system will 
slide eastward beneath rising mid-level heights as the Pacific
trough moves toward the central Rocky Mountains. An increase in
east-northeasterly flow on the southern side of the surface 
high pressure system will shunt the low-level baroclinic zone 
southward. Trapped low-level moisture beneath a persistent 
inversion as well as a steady stream of high clouds from 
convection to our south will maintain cloudy skies throughout 
the day. In fact, would not be surprised to see some areas of 
drizzle particularly in the morning before dry air advection 
allows for the low-level moisture depth to shrink through the 
afternoon hours. Taken altogether, opted to undercut NBM 
temperatures for Wednesday and instead advertise highs in the 
low to mid 60s to perhaps around 70 near the US-24 corridor.
